answer: Amber reached its highest value in the 4th millennium BCE (4000–3001 BCE). It peaked in the time interval BCE 3000–3300 (i.e., CE −3300 to −3000; calBP 4950–5250), where its Z-value attained the global maximum of 1.54 across four consecutive 100-year bins. Boundary note: the BCE 3000 bin (Z=1.54) sits at the very start of the 3rd millennium BCE, while the other three peak bins (BCE 3100/3200/3300) lie in the 4th millennium BCE; the 4th millennium BCE additionally holds the 1.46 high (BCE 3400–4000), so it is unambiguously the millennium of highest amber.

payload.workflow: 1) Loaded data/time_series_data.csv (3601 annual rows, CE -4100..-500, all BCE; calBP=1950-CE) and data/capital.csv (39 rows, BCE 500..4300). 2) Parsed capital.csv's European decimal-comma Zamber by replacing ',' with '.'. 3) Took the raw 100-yr-bin Z-values (time_series `Amber`, capital `Zamber`) as primary and found the global maximum (1.54) and all bins attaining it (BCE 3000/3100/3200/3300). 4) Cross-checked against capital.csv Zamber (identical, max diff 0.00 over 37 overlapping bins) and against time_series `Amber_inter` (same 1.54 plateau, CE -3300..-3000), confirming interpolation does not shift the peak. 5) Mapped the peak bins to millennia using the standard convention (Nth millennium BCE = N*1000..(N-1)*1000+1 BCE): BCE 3100/3200/3300 -> 4th millennium BCE, BCE 3000 -> 3rd millennium BCE; the 4th millennium BCE also holds the 1.46 high (BCE 3400-4000), so it is the millennium of highest amber. 6) Reported the peak interval in BCE, CE(negative) and calBP.
